# The Quiet Sound of Tuesday Morning

I woke up without an alarm today, which means my body has finally accepted that Tuesdays exist whether I acknowledge them or not. The coffee is brewing—that peculiar ritual we perform as though caffeine is the actual reason we get out of bed and not just a convenient excuse. It probably is both.

There's a spider in the corner of my kitchen. I've named her Margaret. She's been there for three days, and I've decided we have an understanding: she doesn't disturb me, and I don't pretend to be the kind of person who kills spiders. This is a compromise I'm comfortable with. Margaret seems satisfied too.

I keep thinking about how we spend so much of our lives doing things that don't actually matter—scrolling through phones, organizing drawers that will just get messy again, replying to emails that generate more emails like some kind of bureaucratic hydra. And yet, there's something oddly comforting about these meaningless rituals. They're the scaffolding holding up days that might otherwise feel too vast and empty to navigate.

My neighbor's dog is barking at something. Possibly nothing. Dogs are philosophers of this sort—they bark at the universe and ask if it's going to answer back. So far, the universe seems content to ignore him, which I think is wisdom on the universe's part.

I've been thinking about a conversation I had with someone at a grocery store last week. We were both reaching for the last container of decent blueberries, and instead of fighting over them like characters in a dystopian novel, we just laughed. I took them, and she made a joke about how I was clearly more berries-desperate than her. I'll never see her again. That moment was the entirety of our relationship. Sometimes I wonder if people remember these small interactions at all, or if they dissolve into the background noise of existence. I remember her, though. I remember her laugh. There's something about randomness that feels sacred.

The news is on in the background. Nothing good, nothing surprising. It's all the same shape it was yesterday, just with different details filling in the template. I've started believing that the news isn't actually meant to inform us but to maintain a baseline of acceptable anxiety. We need to feel worried about something, so we have proof that we're paying attention to the world. It's exhausting.

I should probably be doing something productive right now. That's what the voices in my head keep saying—the chorus of productivity-obsessed culture that's been installed in my brain like a software update I never agreed to. But Tuesday morning feels sacred in its uselessness. The morning is gray. The coffee is hot. Margaret is hunting whatever tiny creatures venture near her web. This is enough.

I've been thinking about how every person walking around the world has an entire, complex interior life. Everyone. The person who was rude to me in the parking lot last week? They probably have seventeen reasons why, none of which have anything to do with me. The barista who misspells my name? Living their own story. We're all walking around inside our own novels, mostly unaware that everyone else is doing the same thing. It's either terrifying or beautiful, depending on what you had for breakfast.

There's a plant on my windowsill that I've been neglecting. It's somehow still alive, which feels like a metaphor for resilience or possibly just poor plant judgment. I should water it. I probably won't. The plant and I will continue this negotiation where I feel guilty and it refuses to die out of spite.

I'm thinking about how we mark time in such arbitrary ways. Tuesdays and Wednesdays and years and decades. None of it's real. Time is real—the flow of moments from past to future—but the containers we put it in are just stories we agreed on. That Tuesday is Tuesday because we said so. There's something absurdly wonderful about that.

I should probably end this. Wrap it up with some kind of conclusion that ties everything together in a neat bow. Some wisdom about the nature of existence or the value of slow mornings or why Margaret the spider is actually a metaphor for accepting difference. But maybe that's not necessary. Maybe the value is in the wandering itself, in the permission to think about random things without having to justify them to some invisible audience.

Though I'm aware that's exactly what I'm doing—I'm thinking out loud to an invisible audience. We're all doing that, all the time, whether we write it down or just let it happen in our heads. We're narrating our lives to someone. Maybe to ourselves. Maybe to the void. Maybe to Margaret, who's definitely smarter than we give her credit for.

The coffee is almost gone. The day is starting to coalesce around me, taking shape. Soon I'll have to do things that mean something—work, probably, or errands, or conversations that require me to be more present than I'm being right now. But for now, in this small window of Tuesday morning, I get to exist in the space between obligation and freedom, between meaning and meaninglessness.

And that, it turns out, is enough.
